1:
What the verse records is a commission and not a choice, and that distinction is pressed by several. Ellicott states it flatly: the selection had been made earlier, and what is described here is the mission of the Twelve, whose number suggested the tribes and marked them as messengers to the whole dispersion. He adds that the title means literally one who is sent, though in classical Greek it had narrowed to a state’s envoy, and that they were sent by him as he had been sent by the Father. Calvin draws the same line: formerly they were selected into his private circle and held in expectation of future labour, where now they are called to immediate performance, given injunctions and endued with power, the hour having come to put their hands to the work — though he notes that perpetual apostleship is not yet in view. Gill makes the same point from their history, that they had been called by grace long since and were more familiar with him than others who went by the name, having heard his doctrine and seen his miracles without yet being sent out. Henry reads the sequence as a principle: the promise that they should be made fishers of men is now performed, and Christ confers honours by degrees, the light of them growing like the light of morning, so that till now he had kept them on probation. Robertson observes that this is the first mention of the group in this Gospel and that the article assumes it already formed, the choosing having preceded the Sermon on the Mount.

The number itself draws more comment than the men. Remigius calls twelve a perfect number because it doubles six, which is perfect in being made of its own parts multiplied into one another. Bede resolves it differently, as three taken four times, so that the faith of the Trinity was to be preached through the four quarters of the world. Rabanus piles up the precedents — the sons of Jacob, the princes of Israel, the springs at Elim, the stones in Aaron’s breastplate, the spies Moses sent, and in the later Scriptures the stars in the bride’s crown and the gates of the city John saw. Lightfoot works on the title, which in his sources marks not merely a messenger but one who represents the person of the sender. Clarke supposes the twelve patriarchs were in view as heads of the congregation of Israel, and Wesley says the same in a line. The Gloss attends to the pairing, that they are named two and two to show them yoke-fellows, and guesses the doubling points to the two precepts of charity or the two Testaments; Barnes supplies from Mark that they were sent out so, each having a companion.

On the power given, the fathers guard the difference between the giver and the agents. Chrysostom notes that he made them confident not only by calling their errand a sending to the harvest but by supplying strength for it. Jerome puts the distinction sharply: a kind master does not grudge his servants a share in his powers, and having cured every sickness himself he imparted the same power — but there is a wide difference between having and imparting, since what he does he does as master, and what they do is done confessing their own weakness in the name of another. Augustine looks at the men chosen, humbly born and without honour or learning, so that whatever great thing they did it was he who was in them and did it; and he notes that one among them was evil, to be used in the Passion and left as an example to the Church of bearing with evil men. Ambrose adds that this was no oversight, since a truth is great which cannot be harmed even by an adversary among its own ministers.
2:
That the title appears here for the first time is noted by three. Gill marks the change of standing behind it: they were learners before, and now, being instructed and sent out to preach publicly, they are called messengers — a word with Jewish precedent, since the elders of the priesthood were called the messengers of the sanhedrim, and messengers were sent by that body through the land and to the captive Jews abroad for half the year. Clarke traces the Greek to a verb meaning to send a message and reports its older political use for a man commissioned by a king to negotiate with another power, so that in Herodotus the word stands level with herald; he adds the observation that Christ’s apostles were first his disciples, which is to say that men must be taught of God before they are sent by him. Robertson calls it the official name and notes that this Gospel gives the names without saying they were chosen at this moment, where Mark and Luke place the choosing after a night of prayer on the mountain, from which he came down to deliver the Sermon. Barnes supplies the same circumstances and locates the mountain near Capernaum.

The order of the list is read for what it implies. Ellicott compares the four catalogues and draws out two facts: Peter stands first in every one and Judas last in every one, the first marking an acknowledged preeminence, and the last perhaps the infamy that came to attach to the traitor — though Ellicott allows the darker possibility, which he thinks may itself have fed the man’s guilt, that his place had always been one of inferiority. He observes too that all four lists fall into three groups of four. Robertson confirms that Simon heads every list. Chrysostom explains the pairing of the first two by different titles, Peter placed from his merit and Andrew from the nobility of being Peter’s brother, and notes that Mark puts Andrew next after Peter and John because Mark arranges by dignity where this writer does not. Calvin turns the same precedence into a controversy: he readily allows that Peter was first among the apostles and denies that what held of a few men can be stretched over the whole world, since being named first implies no authority over his companions — and he ends by granting the whole claim for argument’s sake, which will serve the Roman see nothing until it proves that wicked and sacrilegious apostles are Peter’s successors.

The names themselves are glossed briefly. Barnes explains that Peter means a rock and that he was also called Cephas, a Syro-Chaldaic word of the same force. Lightfoot notes that Simon is the usual Talmudic form of Simeon, the name by which the apostle is also called in the Acts, and that Christ changed the names of exactly those three with whom he kept the closest familiarity, Simon and James and John. Wesley accounts for the word first by attendance rather than rank, since Simon was the first called to constant attendance although Andrew had seen Christ before him. Jerome gives the plainest reason for a catalogue at all, that it was set down so every false apostle should be excluded by it.
3:
Two of these names are suspected of belonging to one man. Gill reports Lightfoot’s conjecture that Bartholomew is Nathanael, since he is listed immediately after Philip, and that the name is Bar Talmai, the son of Talmai or Ptolomy, a name once common to the kings of Egypt. Lightfoot states his own case from the order: set the sequence in which the disciples are called in the fourth Gospel beside the sequence in which they are usually numbered, and Bartholomew falls exactly where Nathanael falls, so that one may think him the same man — called Nathanael by his own name and Bartholomew by his father’s. Clarke reports the same identification as the opinion of many and puts it the same way, that his own name is suppressed here and he is named from his father.

The rest are disposed of in a line or two each. Gill notes that Philip bears a Greek name, which Jewish parents might take from the Greeks living among them, and finds the name in the Jewish writings. Clarke identifies Matthew the publican as the writer of this history, and makes James the son of Alphaeus the same as the Cleopas or Clopas of the later Gospels, married to Mary the sister of the blessed Virgin. Lightfoot observes that the name Alphaeus occurs among the Talmudists too, and that its pronunciation admits of doubt, sounding either Alphai or Cleophi; he supports the Bartholomew identification besides from the Greek translators, who render Talmai as Tolmi, and from the form Tholomaeus in Josephus. Remigius reads the name Thomas for its meaning, an abyss or a twin, which in Greek is Didymus — and he thinks abyss the apter of the two, since the longer that apostle doubted the more deeply he came to believe the effect of the Lord’s passion and the mystery of his Divinity, which forced from him the confession of his Lord and his God. Henry notices what the order costs the writer: elsewhere Matthew stands before Thomas, where in his own catalogue Thomas is put first, which Henry takes for a lesson that the disciples of Christ do well to prefer one another in honour; and where the other lists give the bare name, this one adds the publican, the toll-gatherer called away from an infamous employment to be an apostle — so that those raised to honour with Christ do well to look at the rock they were hewn from.

On the last name the question is why there are two of them. Barnes answers from the languages, that the two forms carry the same meaning in Hebrew and that Luke’s Judas is a slight change from the second of them, such changes being common in all writing. Wesley agrees in substance, giving the man as commonly called Judas, the brother of James. Augustine deals with the variant readings more briskly: some copies have one form and some another, and he asks who ever prevented the same man from having two names, or even three.
4:
Why this Simon carries an epithet is agreed, and what the epithet means is not. Gill explains the addition as distinguishing him from Simon Peter, and denies that it makes him an inhabitant of the land of Canaan in the way a certain woman is called a woman of Canaan, since all the disciples were Jews. Clarke derives the word instead from the Hebrew for zealous, which he says Luke translates literally when he calls the man a Zealot, and guesses the name came of his great fervency in preaching; he also makes him the third son of Alphaeus and so brother to James and Jude. Barnes takes the Zealot title as membership of a small Jewish sect known for its peculiar zeal in religion, and supposes his native place was Cana, so that either title would suit him. Lightfoot points to who the Zealots are in Josephus, and adds a careful remark: if one said this Simon had belonged to that sect before his conversion, the wrong done him would be no greater than the wrong done his fellow-apostle by calling him a publican.

The second name divides them outright. Barnes and Clarke both read it as a place of origin, Barnes making Carioth a small town in the tribe of Judah and Clarke deriving the form from the Hebrew for a man of Kerioth. Wesley puts the birthplace somewhere else entirely, in a town of the tribe of Ephraim near the city of Samaria. Lightfoot declines to settle the derivation and raises a prior question nobody else asks, whether the name was given to the man in his lifetime or only after his death. Gill notes merely that this is the last of the pairs, the whole list being given two by two because they were sent out so.

On the clause that follows the name, two of the fathers refuse to treat it as an accident. Augustine holds that Christ had among the chosen one who was evil, to be used in the accomplishment of the Passion and left as an example to the Church of bearing with evil men. Ambrose puts it as a principle about truth rather than about Judas, that he was not chosen unwittingly, since a truth is great enough to take no harm even from an adversary among its own ministers. Ellicott, counting the lists, observes that the name stands last in all four.
5:
Why they are sent at this moment and not earlier is Chrysostom’s first observation. They had by now seen the dead raised and the sea rebuked and proof enough in word and deed of his power, and only then are they sent; and they are sent to the Jews first so that, trained in Judaea as in a wrestling school, they might afterwards enter the arena of the world — he taught them to fly, Chrysostom says, as one teaches weak nestlings. Gill reads the same readiness from their training, that a long time of private conference and of watching his doctrine and conduct had qualified them for public usefulness, and notes that he sends them in pairs so that each might assist the other and their testimony be joint. The Gloss puts the structure of the charge plainly: having given them the power, he now sends them to use it for others, and in sending tells them where to go, what to preach and what to do. Clarke turns the sending into a list of what any minister needs — the spirit of holiness, a call to the particular work, instruction in its nature, and a commission to testify the Gospel of the grace of God —. Wesley reads the act as a claim of authority, since none but God can authorise men to preach his word, and Robertson notes that the verb for sending is the root of the word apostle.

The restriction is defended on five grounds. Jerome denies any conflict with the later command to teach all nations, since this charge was given before the resurrection and that after, and holds that Christ had to be preached to the Jews first so they could not plead that they had been passed over for Gentiles and Samaritans. Gregory makes the same point from the other end: the Redeemer’s preaching should appear to seek foreign lands only because it had been refused at home. Hilary grounds the priority in the Law, since the nation that received its promulgation earned the first preaching of the Gospel and would have the less excuse for its crime, having had the more warning. Calvin confines the commission to its purpose, which was to awaken in the Jews the hope of an approaching salvation and make them attend to Christ, the voice being limited now to Judea and afterwards commanded to sound to the ends of the earth, because he had been sent to be the minister of circumcision and fulfil promises anciently given. Robertson and Wesley both make the limit temporary — for this tour only, so as to give the Jews the first opportunity and not prejudice the cause at this stage, the calling of the Gentiles waiting on the fuller gift of the Spirit.

Samaria gets separate treatment. Lightfoot explains that the Jews’ privileges were to be reserved to them until they forfeited them by their own perverseness, and grants the Samaritans a real case: they claimed descent from Jacob, which he says was not altogether far from the truth, they held the law of Moses, and they looked for the Messiah as the Jews did. Barnes places them in the country that had belonged to Ephraim and half of Manasseh. Wesley draws the limit narrowly, that they were not to enter in order to preach, though they might to buy what they needed. Ellicott feels the difficulty most sharply, since the same Gospel speaks of those who shall come from east and west, and Christ had already taken these men into a Samaritan city and shown them fields white to harvest there; his answer is that the prohibition belonged to this mission and no further. Jerome adds a figurative reading, that those who bear the name of Christ are told not to walk in the way of the Gentiles nor in the error of the heretics.
6:
Who the house of Israel is gets a careful answer. Gill begins from the fact that this is the flock to whom Christ himself was sent, and notes that the phrase, when set against the house of Judah, means only the ten tribes, but here takes in the whole nation then living in Judaea, among whom there were some of every tribe; and the lost sheep he understands of the people generally, wandering and lost in error and sin. Barnes reads the image as pity rather than reproach, a flock straying without a shepherd, and gives their history as the reason for the priority: they had been the chosen people, they had long looked for the Messiah, and it was proper the gospel should be offered to them first. Clarke works the same figure harder — the Jewish Church was the ancient fold of God, the sheep had wandered from their Shepherd and were lost, and these under-shepherds are sent to seek them, find them, and bring them back to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls.

Robertson is careful about the tone. The phrase is the sheep, the lost ones, and he insists, with Bruce, that it is used not in blame but in pity; he cites Bengel for the observation that Christ says lost more often than he says led astray, and McNeile for the judgment that if the nation could be brought to repentance the new age would dawn. Calvin explains the double purpose of the wording: the apostles, hearing the people called lost, would be moved by compassion to run to their help the more warmly, and would learn at the same time that there was abundant occasion for their labour. He grounds the precedence itself not in merit but in standing, since the Jews were the firstborn, or rather since at that time they alone were acknowledged to belong to God’s family while the rest stood removed and banished from it. Hilary alone lets an edge into it, remarking that those called sheep here raged against Christ with the tongues and throats of wolves and vipers.
7:
The commission is read as an itinerant one. Gill has them moving through the cities of Judaea and their streets, from one town to another, since these were travelling preachers who were not to settle anywhere but to keep moving so the Gospel might cover the land. Clarke renders the words as a command to proclaim while proceeding — preach and travel, and as you travel preach — and adds that Christ’s ministers find ruined souls wherever they go and should proclaim his power to save wherever they find them. Robertson notes the present participle and present imperative and calls them heralds on a preaching tour; the message is the same summary that the Baptist had startled the country with, and they are to shake Galilee with it as Christ had done.

The words themselves are treated as a set formula. Ellicott observes that they repeat exactly what had described first the Baptist’s teaching and then our Lord’s, which suggests an actual form of proclamation, and he pictures the procedure: the King’s two envoys enter a town, stand in the gate, announce that his kingdom has come near, and then, the crowd having gathered, call men to the repentance without which they cannot enter it. Barnes renders the clause more literally as the reign of heaven drawing near. Clarke draws from the commission what the grand subject of apostolic preaching was, and Robertson remarks that the same astonishing message is as much needed now.

What the announcement was meant to do is Calvin’s question. It was to rouse the nation to expect an approaching redemption, and to teach three things at once: that their restoration was owed to divine agency and not to any human kindness, that under the reign of God their condition would be prosperous, and that the happiness promised them was not earthly and fading but heavenly and lasting. Rabanus adds a caution about the verb, that the kingdom is said to draw near by the faith in the unseen Creator which is given us, and not by any movement of the visible elements; and he reads the heavens of the phrase as the saints, who contain God by faith and love him with affection.
8:
One clause of this commission is disputed as text rather than doctrine. Clarke reports that the command to raise the dead is missing from a long list of manuscripts and versions and from three of the fathers, observes that there is no evidence the disciples raised anyone before the resurrection of Christ, and concludes the words should be omitted unless the authority given here reached beyond the present mission. Ellicott agrees that the best manuscripts omit them and that their absence suits the history better, since no instance of that highest kind of miracle is recorded of the disciples during our Lord’s ministry, it being reserved for his own act; he guesses the words were inserted by someone who wished the command to cover the later raisings in the Acts.

On the powers themselves the comment is practical. Gill notes that the commission matched the power already given, and that nothing could prove their mission divine and their doctrine heavenly, or recommend them better to men, than healing sick friends whom physicians had given up — and healing them without medicine, by a word or a touch of the hands. Calvin reads the miracles as a declaration of purpose: the power was lodged with them for the common benefit and they are charged to be liberal and not to suppress it, and the direction of it tells why he was sent and what his Gospel was for, since he enjoins healing rather than the bringing of disease on the healthy or death on the living. Remigius turns each of the four into a spiritual condition — the sick are the slothful who lack strength to live well, the lepers the unclean in sin and carnal delight, the possessed those given up to the power of the Devil. Wesley takes up the last of them as a controversy, noting how readily an unbeliever is relieved to hear a learned man observe that the diseases ascribed here to the devil show the same symptoms as natural lunacy or epilepsy or convulsions, and to conclude from that the devil had no hand in them; he answers by asking what would follow if God permitted an evil spirit to work under the very same symptoms.

The closing rule is read as a prohibition of trade. Barnes states it plainly: they were not to sell their healing or their preaching, nor make a money-making business of it by bargaining to cure for a price — which, he is careful to add, never barred them then or later from a competent support. Cyril presses the same rule through the story of Gehazi, who sold the cure of a leper and received the leprosy for his inheritance, the prophet having fulfilled the bidding to give freely what he had freely received while his servant sold the grace and so took the terms of his own sale.
9:
What the prohibition covers is settled first. Gill takes the three metals as standing for money of every kind, since coin was struck in all three, from sums of consequence down to the brass halfpence and farthings that are least worth having. Ellicott notes that Luke names silver only and Mark the copper, where this report takes in all three forms then current. Robertson insists on the exact force of the verb: it is not do not possess but do not acquire or procure, and he reads the three metals as a descending scale. Ellicott makes the same grammatical point and draws the practical consequence, that if they had money already they might take it, but they were not to get any as a condition of setting out, still less to wait until they had got it; Wesley puts the stress on the same word, that they might use what lay ready but must not delay a moment to provide more. Barnes and Clarke both explain the purse as the girdle, Barnes describing it as hollow and an indispensable part of the dress, Clarke correcting the common account from his own observation, that easterners carry money not in a fold of the girdle but in a purse in the bosom beneath it. Lightfoot adds that the things forbidden here were simply the ordinary provision of travellers, to which the more religious added a copy of the law.

Why it was imposed divides into the temporary and the permanent. Calvin makes it a matter of speed: the embassy was to cross the whole of Judaea within a few days and return, so luggage that would slow them is forbidden — and he says bluntly that some have ignorantly taken a rule laid down for this errand as a perpetual law for ministers. Wesley agrees on the reason and adds a second, that they were to learn by it to trust God in every future strait. Chrysostom reads it as a purging of motive: having forbidden the sale of spiritual things, Christ now pulls up the root of the evil, and the precept frees them from suspicion, frees them from distraction so that their whole time goes to preaching, and marks their excellence besides — which is why he could ask them later whether anything had been lacking when he sent them without bag or purse. Chrysostom calls it a happy exchange, power received in the place of gold and silver. Jerome reasons from the same ground and goes further: if they preached without payment, wealth was simply unnecessary, and had they carried it they would have been thought to preach for their own gain rather than men’s salvation; having cut off riches he now cuts away even the necessaries, so that men who taught that God’s providence directs everything should be seen taking no thought for the morrow.

Three readings take the equipment figuratively. The Gloss distinguishes the two kinds of provision the charge forbids, the means of buying necessaries in the purse and the necessaries themselves in the bag. Hilary makes the girdle the readiness and activity of the ministry, so that forbidding money in it warns against letting anything in that ministry be bought and sold. Remigius finds in the whole prohibition a restoration, the holy preachers being set back in the dignity of the first man, who desired nothing else while he still held the heavenly treasures and began to crave other things only when he had lost them by sinning. Augustine states the limit on the other side: the Gospel is not for sale and they who sell it sell a great thing cheap, so let preachers take their necessary support from the people and their reward from God — what the people give being not pay for a service but a stipend that frees them to work.
10:
The scrip is described before it is forbidden. Gill gives its Jewish name and calls it a large leathern bag in which shepherds and travellers carried food, slung about the neck; Clarke gives the same name and the same description and adds that it was properly the shepherd’s bag. Barnes calls it a knapsack of skin or coarse cloth for provisions, likewise hung round the neck, and explains the prohibition by the provision promised on the road, which made a store unnecessary. Ellicott, noting that the English word has gone out of use, describes a small basket carried on the back or slung from one shoulder, and recalls that David carried five smooth stones from the brook in his; the point he draws is that such a basket was reckoned the necessary equipment of even the poorest traveller, and the apostles were to go without it. Lightfoot reports that the Syriac renders the word purse, and quotes a proselyte who speaks of the stranger coming with his staff and his pouch.

The coats and the shoes raise questions of degree and of harmony. Lightfoot explains that one coat bespoke a meaner condition and two a more comfortable one, which is why the Baptist had told the man with two to share with the man who had none. Clarke reduces the clause to its principle, that they were to carry nothing that would encumber them, and reports on the staff that where the common text has the singular a long list of manuscripts, versions and two of the fathers read the plural. Barnes meets the apparent contradiction with Mark, who has them shod with sandals where this verse forbids shoes, and holds that the original word here is the one commonly rendered sandals, so that the difference is apparent only and not real.

The reason given at the end turns the whole charge round. It rests the apostles’ maintenance not on what they carry but on what their work entitles them to, so that the prohibition of provisions is also a promise of them — which is why Barnes can explain the empty knapsack by the certainty of being provided for on the way, and why Hilary can say of the two coats that one is enough.
11:
Why a host had to be chosen at all follows from what went before. Chrysostom connects it to the promise of maintenance: lest they should suppose every door would be opened to them, they are told to use much circumspection, and he anticipates the obvious objection by asking how Christ himself then lodged with a publican — the answer being that conversion had made the man worthy, since the requirement bears on character and not on rank. Jerome explains the practical difficulty, that men entering a strange town could not know what each inhabitant was, and so had to choose by the report of the people and the opinion of the neighbours, lest the preacher’s standing be disgraced by his entertainer’s bad name; and he turns the transaction round, so that the host chosen does not so much confer a favour as receive one. Clarke makes the same point, that a preacher must be careful of his reputation and lodge only with people of regular life. Ellicott adds the local reason: eastern habits of hospitality would throw open many houses that offered no opening for the work or would bring an evil report, so they were to pass those by and find someone poor but well spoken of who would receive them as bearers of good news. Calvin reads the instruction as an answer to a worry, that nobody would acknowledge them and they would lose the food they were entitled to; the remedy is to enquire in each place whether there are godly and upright men with some reverence for God, of whom good hope may be had, and to direct their labour chiefly to those.

The order to stay put is read as a guard against several faults at once. Barnes supplies Luke’s blunter form, not to go from house to house, and gives the reasons: they were to content themselves with one house, not wander like vagrants or beggars, not appear to be men of idleness. Clarke says that acting against this precept has often brought great disgrace on the Gospel. Wesley compresses it to a line, that they were to abide in that house till they left the town. Gill notes that the instruction answers where to go and whom to ask for, the manner of their travelling having been settled already.

The salutation and its refusal are given their spiritual weight. The Gloss reads the greeting as a prayer that peace may come on the master of the house and all resistance to the truth be pacified. Remigius draws out the alternative outcomes: either the hearer, being appointed to eternal life, follows the heavenly word when he hears it, or, if nobody will hear, the preacher is still not without fruit, since his peace returns to him when he receives his wages from the Lord; and he reads the offer of peace as the very means by which a worthy house was to be identified. Hilary keeps a distinction between the word and the gift, so that peace seems spoken rather than given, the apostles’ own peace not resting on an unworthy house but the sacrament of heavenly peace being kept within their own breast. Ambrose warns them not to choose carelessly, so as to have no cause to change lodgings, and notes that no such caution is laid on the host, lest hospitality be narrowed by a man picking his guests. On the shaking of the dust Rabanus offers a figure: the feet of the disciples mean the labour and progress of preaching, and the dust on them the lightness of earthly thoughts, from which even the greatest teachers are not free, since anxiety for their hearers draws them into cares and they gather the dust of the roads they walk — so that those who despised such teachers turn all the toil and danger of the apostles into a witness against themselves.
12:
What the house is, and which house is meant, are settled together. Gill takes it for the house of the hospitable man already found by enquiry, the article pointing back to that search. Ellicott objects to the English indefinite article as misleading and insists we must read the house, that is, the dwelling of the man reported worthy. Barnes reads the word as meaning the family rather than the building, citing the usage elsewhere of a man believing with his whole house, and takes the command accordingly: the apostles were to greet the family and show them the customary tokens of respect. He draws a general rule from that, that religion never requires or permits its friends to outrage the common rules of social intercourse but demands the proper courtesies of all.

The form of the greeting is supplied from Luke and from the manuscripts. Ellicott gives it as the familiar peace be with thee, or peace be to this house, which he says the words that follow imply. Wesley gives the same in the usual Jewish form, glossing peace as all blessings. Clarke reports the textual position in detail: the explanatory clause naming the words of the salutation is, as he says, necessary to the connection in which it now stands, and is added by a long list of manuscripts and by the Armenian, Ethiopic, Slavonic, Saxon and Vulgate, by all the copies of the old Itala and by two of the fathers, and is found in several modern versions besides, which he illustrates from the Greek and Italian of his own day.

Calvin explains why a general greeting was commanded when a careful choice had already been made. The apostles could not tell true worshippers of God from despisers, so they are told to address any family they happen to meet in a friendly way, a salutation being a kind of opening to conversation. They had indeed been warned to look out for hosts whose religious zeal was commonly known; but since men of lofty reputation sometimes betray their impiety when brought to a serious test, Calvin holds it proper that this further rule should be added.
13:
The conditional troubles Ellicott, and he says so. The doubt implied in the word if looks at first inconsistent with the supposition that they entered only after satisfying themselves about the occupant; his answer is that the missionaries came into each town as strangers, where even the most careful enquiry might fail. He takes the peace of the clause to be the peace of the salutation itself, and reads the imperative as less a command than a declaration of what will follow. Gill describes the worthy house concretely, as one whose master proved civil and courteous and hospitable on being greeted, and ready to receive them and provide for them. Clarke puts the same test in two parts, whether the family is a proper lodging for a preacher and whether its head is ready to embrace the message of salvation. Robertson asks the question directly and answers it from McNeile, that what naturally makes a house worthy is readiness to receive the preachers and their message; he adds that hospitality is among the noblest graces and that the apostles were not to be burdensome as guests.

What the peace amounts to, and what becomes of it when refused, is where they differ in emphasis. Barnes reads it as the happiness they had prayed for in saluting, and makes the apostles instruments of it by prayer and instruction and by remaining in the house to impart the blessings of the gospel. Clarke takes it as a material promise as well, that God will prosper such a family in their bodies and souls and substance. On the refusal both have the blessing revert: Clarke renders the Greek as turning back upon the speakers, so that the household gets nothing while the apostles lose nothing, and Barnes reads the unwillingness to receive them as the condition on which the peace returns.

Calvin paraphrases the withdrawal as an instruction to break off every bond of communication, since ingratitude has made such people unworthy to enjoy the blessing that was asked for them. He then limits how much should be read into the word: it refers to the ordinary Jewish salutation, in which the Hebrew term is used to wish a man well and prosperous and his affairs successful; and although Calvin grants that the apostles brought men a peace of another kind, he calls it too fine a speculation to make this passage speak of the free reconciliation between God and men.
14:
The gesture is explained from Jewish practice, and every one of them explains it the same way. Lightfoot cites the schools of the scribes, who taught that the dust of a heathen land defiled by the touch, and quotes the ruling that the dust of Syria defiles like the dust of other heathen countries, with a further debate about bringing herbs into Israel from abroad for fear of the dust that comes with them. Barnes says the Jews taught uniformly that Gentile dust was impure and to be shaken off, so that the act declared the people impure and profane and unworthy of instruction, and broke off all further connection; he notes that the apostles were afterwards recorded doing it. Clarke gives the same with the prophetic background, that a heathen country was held a polluted land against the holy land of Israel, so that shaking its dust from clothes or feet renounced all further dealing and set the place on a level with heathen cities. Wesley describes the custom concretely — Jews returning from abroad stopped at the border and wiped the dust from their feet so the holy land should not be polluted — and draws the sting: the act told those Jews who refused the Gospel that they were holy no longer but stood level with idolaters. Ellicott calls it a protest in act, declaring what our Lord declares in words, that a house or city refusing the King’s messengers was below the level even of the Gentiles.

Robertson adds the physical force and one correction. The verb is to shake out, a rather violent gesture of disfavour; and the Jewish horror of the smallest particle of Gentile dust had nothing to do with disease, of which they knew nothing, but came of regarding such dust as the putrescence of death. He also marks the scope, that this too was a restriction belonging to the special tour.

Calvin reads the sentence as consolation rather than as instruction. The threat against the despisers of the gospel was meant to animate the disciples so that the ingratitude of the world should not slow them; and although it does tell them what to do when they meet contempt, its principal design was that wherever their doctrine was refused their grief, well founded as it was, should be relieved, and they should not fail in the middle of their course. Calvin points to Paul as a man who leaned on that consolation and could afterwards set contempt at nothing. Gill, for his part, defines the refusal narrowly, as a refusal to take them in and provide for them in a friendly manner.
15:
What the comparison asserts is agreed and sharply put. Ellicott says the thought implied in the previous verse is here stated outright: the cities that stood out in the history of the world as the most infamous of all were nevertheless less guilty, because they sinned against less light, than those who rejected the King’s messengers; and he notes the same comparison returning later with Tyre and Sidon added. Barnes gives the history of those cities, destroyed with two others by fire and brimstone or by a volcanic eruption for their great wickedness, on ground afterwards covered by the Dead Sea, and gives the same reason for the verdict, that they had not been favoured with so much light and instruction. Robertson handles the comparative with a lighter touch, noting that the papyri use the word of a convalescent and that people still say they feel tolerable, and sums the matter up by observing that the Galileans were enjoying more privileges than Sodom and Gomorrah ever had.

What the day of judgment means is where they part. Clarke doubts it is the general judgment at all, and doubts equally that it means the destruction of the Jewish state by the Romans; he takes it for a day on which God should send punishment on that particular city or person for their crimes, just as the day of judgment for Sodom was the day it was destroyed from heaven. Ellicott takes the opposite view of the phrase, that like the day of the Lord in the older Scriptures it ranges wider than any single event. Calvin reports the same reading Clarke prefers, that some understand it of the destruction of Jerusalem, and calls it foreign to the passage; what matters to him is that the threat should not be taken for an idle bugbear, a thing said only to frighten children, since Christ is declaring in earnest that those who reject the gospel will be punished more severely than the men of Sodom.

Gill marks what the sentence adds to what has gone before. It was not enough that such despisers should forfeit the peace the apostles had wished them and be declared level with heathen cities; everlasting punishment in the world to come is now asserted of them, and asserted, Gill says, in the strongest manner Christ could use.
16:
Why the warning comes at this point is Chrysostom’s question, and he gives five reasons. Having freed them from care and armed them with miraculous powers, Christ foretells the evils that will befall them: so that they might know he knew the future; so that they should not suppose the troubles came of any want of power in their Master; so that they should not be astonished by a blow they had not expected; so that, having heard it beforehand, they should not lose heart at the season of his cross; and lastly for a reason he adds to the rest. Gill reads the scope of the prediction more widely than the present errand, taking this and what follows to concern chiefly the troubles that came after the death and resurrection, when their commission was enlarged and they were sent out afresh — a faithful account given beforehand so they should be prepared and not surprised. Henry says the same, that the passage looks beyond this mission, since they met no great hardship while Christ was with them and were not well able to bear any.

The two animals of the comparison are worked over in turn. Jerome identifies the wolves as the scribes and Pharisees, the clergy of the Jews, and reads the serpent’s craft as an example in one particular only: it hides its head with the whole of its body to protect the part in which its life is, and so we should expose the whole body to guard our head, which is Christ, keeping the faith whole and uncorrupt. Rabanus takes the serpent differently, as one that seeks out narrow chinks to crawl through and so works off its old skin, which is the preacher passing through the narrow way and laying aside the old man; and he notes that the wolves meant men, since the next clause says to take heed of men. Hilary makes the wolves all who should pursue the apostles with mad fury, and then turns the serpent’s method into method for preachers: the tempter began with the softer sex, allured her with hope and promised a share of immortality, so they in like manner should seize every opportunity, study each man’s nature and inclination, use wisdom of speech and hold out hope of good things — preaching truly what the other promised falsely. Remigius explains why the serpent at all: the first man was beguiled by one, so the foe is subtle to deceive and they must be wise to rescue, and where he commended a tree they are to commend the tree of the Cross. He adds the reason the two are joined, that simplicity without wisdom is easily deceived and wisdom is dangerous unless tempered by a simplicity that hurts nobody.

Gregory applies the charge to the office rather than the danger. A man who undertakes to preach ought not to do evil but to suffer it, softening the anger of the angry by his meekness and healing the wounds of sinners by his own; and if the zeal of right-doing ever requires severity toward those under him, that severity must be of love and not of cruelty, keeping the rights of discipline outwardly while inwardly loving those it corrects. The Gloss, meanwhile, reads the need for serpentine wisdom straight off the following clauses, since they will be delivered to councils and forbidden to preach in that name, and then scourged if they are not corrected, and at length brought before kings and governors.
17:
Which men they are to beware of is narrowed by most of them. Gill calls the phrase uncommon and emphatic and takes it to mean not merely wicked men at large but chiefly men of note and authority, the ecclesiastical and civil governors of the people — scribes, Pharisees, elders, chief priests and the rest — so that the advice is to take care how they came into such company. Clarke reads it as their own countrymen, from whom they might reasonably have expected comfort and support, and especially those in power who would abuse it to oppress them. Robertson notes the construction, which is to hold the mind away from, and points out that the article looks back to the wolves of the previous verse. Barnes takes the warning as a call for ordinary prudence, that they were not to run needlessly into danger nor needlessly endanger their lives. Wesley puts the same thought as a corrective: they were not to imagine that all their innocence and all their wisdom would screen them from persecution.

The councils and the scourging are identified from Jewish institutions. Ellicott argues from the plural that the Great Council at Jerusalem is not meant but the lesser councils attached to provincial synagogues, which had power to judge and punish men accused of offences against religion. Robertson agrees, calling them the local courts of justice in every Jewish town, and notes that the Greek word is an old one used from Herodotus onward for any deliberative body, the same word serving for the Sanhedrin itself. Barnes allows both senses, that the word commonly means the great national council but here seems to mean any judicial tribunal, of which there were some in every village. Clarke explains that by synagogues we are to understand not the places of public worship but assemblies where three magistrates, chosen from the principal members, presided to settle differences. Wesley says the same, that the Jews held their courts for both civil and ecclesiastical affairs in them.

Ellicott and Lightfoot both face the oddity of a punishment inflicted inside a place of worship. Ellicott takes the words to imply that the scourging actually happened within the walls of the building, grants that this looks to us something like desecration, and sees no reason to think it looked so to the Jews. Lightfoot reports that Beza, unable to explain the case, suspected the text, since he could find neither synagogues elsewhere named from houses of judgment nor civil punishments carried out in them; and Lightfoot answers that the suspicion has no cause, since every synagogue had its civil triumvirate of three magistrates who judged matters in contest arising within it. Calvin spends his note on a smaller question of translation, reporting that Erasmus inserted a word on the supposition that the article here carries the force of a demonstrative and so points to some particular men.
18:
The audience named here is taken as a widening of the commission. Ellicott marks the words as significant for looking forward, on the assumption that the discourse is one piece, to the work among the Gentiles which the Twelve had just been told they were not yet to enter; and he fixes the terms, that rulers always stands in these writings for the governors of the Roman Empire — proconsuls, procurators and the like — while kings at least includes, and may chiefly mean, the emperors themselves. Clarke reads them the same way, as the Roman proconsuls and governors of provinces together with the kings tributary to Rome. Gill explains why Roman officers come into it at all: judgments touching life and death had been taken away from the Jewish council, by their own account forty years before the destruction of the second temple, which Gill notes falls much about the time of Christ’s death, so that what power remained to them reached only to lesser matters and lesser punishments, beating and scourging; and he lists Paul before Gallio and Felix and Festus as the fulfilment.

Barnes treats the prediction as a thing to be checked against the record, and calls it completely and abundantly fulfilled, citing a string of appearances in the Acts and adding the tradition that Peter was brought before one Roman emperor and John before another, with others before Parthian and Scythian and Indian kings. Clarke draws from the same fulfilment an argument about foreknowledge, quoting Wakefield for the question who could have thought at the time that such despised and illiterate men would draw so much attention and be called on to defend their faith before the most illustrious persons on earth.

On the last clause two of them agree in correcting the English. Barnes notes that the phrase may be rendered not against them but to them, so that the apostles stood there as witnesses to those rulers of the great facts and doctrines of the Christian religion. Ellicott makes the same correction more briefly, that the word is simply unto rather than against.
19:
The promise is read first as an answer to a fear. Gill sets out the fear exactly: men who had heard they would be delivered to councils and brought before governors and kings might well wonder what they could say in their own defence and in defence of the truth, being unlearned men of no elocution and mean birth, most of them poor fishermen. Barnes says the same and adds the eastern background, that kings were regarded as raised far above common mortals and approaching the divine, which makes the assurance the more consoling. Robertson quotes two judgments to the same effect, that self-defence before Jewish kings and heathen governors would be a terrible ordeal for humble Galileans, and that it might alarm the bravest of these simple fishermen to be told they must answer for their conduct before such courts; he is careful to add that the injunction applied to cases where preparing a speech would be impossible. Ellicott hears an almost tender sympathy in the words and finds in them a double promise, covering not only what they should say but the form and phrase in which to say it.

What the prohibition does and does not forbid is guarded on both sides. Clarke renders it as being not anxiously careful, since such anxiety argues distrust of God and infallibly produces a confused mind, in which state no man is fit to proclaim or vindicate the truth; but he insists the promise banishes distrust without encouraging sloth, and without releasing anyone from the duty of preparing by meditation on sacred truth. Ellicott reads it in the same sense as the earlier charge about anxiety, as a command not to be over-anxious at that moment. Robertson parses it as an ingressive aorist, do not become anxious, and says plainly that Christ is not talking about something else. Wesley limits it to the sudden call, that neither then nor on any such occasion need they be careful how or what to answer.

The fathers press the promise further than consolation. Chrysostom counts it another and not a small topic of comfort, meeting the objection how such men could ever be persuaded, and finds in it a raising of the apostles to the dignity of the prophets, who spoke by the Spirit of God. Remigius distinguishes the two words of the clause, one bearing on the substance and the other on the expression, and since both were to be supplied there was no need for anxiety about either: they go out to the battle, he says, but it is Christ who fights; they utter the words, but it is he who speaks — which is why Paul could ask for a proof of the Christ who spoke in him. Jerome puts the same economy as a division of labour, that we are to offer only our will for Christ while Christ who dwells in us speaks for himself and the grace of the Spirit ministers the answer. Hilary grounds the confidence in a precedent, that faith keeping all the precepts of the divine will shall be furnished with an answer according to knowledge, as Abraham, having given up Isaac, did not lack a ram for the victim. Calvin states what the promise secures, that the exhortations would have been given in vain had God not been promised with them, and infers that announcing such dangers was never meant to cool the zeal with which the disciples had to burn.
20:
How strongly the clause should be taken is the question. Ellicott calls the words strong, so that human thoughts and purposes seem utterly suppressed and only the inspiring agency is recognised; and he enters a caution at once, that it would be beside the drift of the discourse to make a promise of special aid in moments of special danger into the groundwork of a theory of inspiration covering the written records of the disciples’ work. Gill guards the same point from the other side: not that they were not to speak the words, for they did speak them, but that both the matter and the very words were suggested and dictated by the Spirit of God, since the preparing of the heart in them and the answer of the tongue by them were alike from the Lord — the Spirit the efficient cause, they only the instruments.

Clarke measures how far the promise reaches. He calls it extraordinary and literally fulfilled in those first preachers, to whom it was essentially necessary because the whole dispensation of the New Testament was to be opened by their extraordinary inspiration; and then he allows a lesser sense in which it may still be truly said that the Holy Spirit animates the true disciples of Christ and enables them to speak, the Head speaking in his members by his Spirit, since it is the province of the Spirit of God to speak for God. On that footing Clarke holds that neither surprise, nor want of talent, nor even ignorance itself could hurt the cause of God in those primitive days, while such men’s hearts and minds were under that influence; and he notes that the title Father is added here expressly to excite and increase their confidence. Cyril uses the title in this clause as one item in a larger argument about names. His thesis is that one and the same person is meant under several designations — Holy Ghost, Comforter, Spirit of Truth, and here the Father’s own — and he establishes each identification from a saying of Christ or of Paul: the Comforter is named the Holy Ghost outright, the promise of another Comforter to abide for ever calls him by the third title, the descent at the baptism and the statement that those so led are God’s sons supply a fourth, and the words before us supply the last
21:
That the warning is domestic is what every one of them fastens on. The Gloss notes the order of the discourse, that the comfort came first and the more alarming perils are added after it. Gill reads the progression the same way: having fortified their minds with promises of divine assistance, Christ now opens more largely the sorrows attending a faithful ministry, and the point of this one is that the true followers of Christ should be betrayed not only by strangers but by their own. Calvin states the principle most exactly: the circumstances which other men find to be means of protection, or from which they get some relief, will prove to the disciples a fresh addition to their misery, since those who ought to help them when oppressed and watch over their safety will be their mortal enemies. Gregory explains why that cuts deeper, that wrongs suffered from strangers pain us less than wrongs from men on whose affection we had counted, because besides the bodily affliction there is the pain of affection lost. Jerome says the thing is often seen in persecutions, and gives the reason, that there is no true affection between men whose faith differs.

Two of the moderns treat the prediction as a thing almost incredible until history confirmed it. Barnes says that were there no evidence it had happened it could scarcely be believed, the ties binding brothers and parents and children being so strong that division of sentiment in religion could hardly be thought to overcome them — and yet history assures us it has, from which he infers how awful the malignity of the human heart must be. Clarke turns the same fact into an outcry, asking what astonishing enmity against God and goodness there must be in the soul of man that men should think they did God service by killing those who differed from them in a political or religious creed, a thing he says cannot be accounted for except by an indescribable depravity; and he quotes the poet’s reproach that devils damned keep firm concord where rational creatures alone disagree. Ellicott notes that the Greek has the nouns without the article, brother shall deliver up brother, which he thinks the more forcible as a statement of what would often happen, and observes that the words reproduce almost verbally a prophecy of Micah, where they are followed by the prophet’s resolve to look to the Lord and wait for the God of his salvation — which answers to the endurance promised here.
22:
The breadth of the hatred is qualified rather than softened. Barnes reads all men as all kinds of men, the human heart being set against the apostles because it is set against Christ. Gill applies the clause more particularly to the apostles themselves, where what went before concerned Christ’s followers generally, since they were to be not merely ill treated along with others by relations whose love had turned to hatred, but made the very mark of the malice of all men. Clarke supplies the reason from the other side, that the world hates them because they are attached to Christ and saved from the corruption that is in it, the laws of Christ condemning a vicious world and galling it to revenge. Robertson notes the periphrastic future, by which the hatred goes on through the ages, and that the name stands for the person. Ellicott finds in the clause a precision that attests divine foreknowledge: from the days of Stephen to the last martyr under Diocletian it was always as a Christian and for the name of Christ that men suffered, and would they only have renounced that, all would have gone smoothly — which he supports from Tertullian’s account of the sufferers of his own day.

On the promise to those who endure, the comment converges on the end rather than the beginning. Chrysostom warns that many are hot and zealous at first and afterwards grow cool, and has Christ answer that it is the end he looks at, asking what profit there is in seed that only sprouts for a while. Remigius states the rule flatly, that the reward belongs not to those who begin but to those who finish, so that whoever neither lets go the commands of the faith nor falls away under persecution shall be saved and receive the heavenly kingdom for his earthly persecutions. He then opens a second sense, noting that the end does not always mean destruction but sometimes perfection, as when Christ is called the end of the Law, so that enduring to the end may mean enduring in Christ; and Augustine supplies the definition, that to endure in Christ is to abide in his faith which works by love. Barnes takes the plainer sense, the end of life, be it longer or shorter, and makes the endurance the decisive evidence of attachment. Clarke adds a historical reading beside it, that the man who holds fast faith and a good conscience until the threatened punishment falls on that wicked people shall be preserved.
23:
That flight is permitted, and even commanded, is what strikes them first. Chrysostom notes the turn in the discourse, that after foretelling fearful things to come after the cross and resurrection and ascension Christ leads them to gentler prospects, and does not bid them offer themselves presumptuously to persecution but fly from it, adapting his words to men who were only at the beginning of their course. Gill reads it as a rule of usefulness: when a city would not let them go on with their work they were not to desist but to go elsewhere, where they might hope for a better reception and do more good. Barnes states the limits on both sides, that they were not permitted to throw away their lives and were to preserve them where that could be done without denying their Lord, yet that all Christ’s commands show they were rather to die than deny him. Ellicott takes the counsel as one form of the serpent’s wisdom commanded earlier, so that men were not to imagine they were enduring to the end when in the eagerness of their zeal they courted martyrdom, but were to avoid danger and use every opportunity to keep the work going; and he traces the effect of the command through the great Roman persecutions in the conduct of Polycarp and Cyprian. Clarke calls it prudence to avoid persecution where charity permits,.

Augustine answers the question the permission raises, whether it implies any weakness in the protector. It is not that the Saviour could not shield his disciples that he bids them fly and sets them the example, but that he was instructing human frailty not to presume on God while it has something it can do for itself; and he presses it from the other extreme, that Christ neither commanded nor allowed escape by laying violent hands on themselves, so flight is the way left open. Remigius divides the counsel by the strength of those who receive it, so that the precept of endurance belongs properly to the apostles and their successors, men of fortitude, while the permission to fly suits the weak in faith, whom a tender Master spares lest they offer themselves for martyrdom and deny the faith under the pain — the sin of flight being lighter than the sin of denial. Jerome sets the whole saying in its first context, the mission on which they were told not to go to the Gentiles, and notes that the believers did exactly this at the start, being scattered through Judaea by the persecution at Jerusalem, so that the season of tribulation became the seedtime of the Gospel.

The closing clause is the difficulty, and nobody pretends to have settled it. Robertson lists the readings without choosing: some take it of this Galilean tour, which Christ might overtake; others of the Transfiguration, others of the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost, others of the Second Coming; some hold the saying has been put in the wrong context. Rabanus reads it as a prediction that they would not have brought all the cities of Israel to the faith before the resurrection was accomplished and a wider commission given. Lightfoot takes it the same way, glossing it as not having travelled through the cities of Israel preaching before the Son of man is revealed by his rising. Hilary reads it of a longer history, the preaching driven from Judaea into Greece and thence, worn by sufferings up and down the Greek cities, taking lasting refuge among the rest of the Gentiles, while the remnant of Israel believes only at the second coming. Calvin treats the verse as answering an objection — if the resentment of the whole world must be faced, what will the end be? — and finds the answer in a charge not to despair but, when driven from one place, to try another.
24:
The proverb is identified before it is applied. Ellicott thinks it was probably a common saying, and notes that our Lord uses it elsewhere with more than one application; here the sense is that they should not be amazed or cast down by these prophecies of evil days, since in all their sufferings they would only be following in his footsteps, and what had been said and done to him would be said and done to them. Clarke restates it in plainer terms, that a scholar is not above his teacher, and says the saying needs no comment since its reasonableness is self-evident — what needs attention is its spirit, for a man who keeps it in his heart will never complain of what he suffers, and it is capable of restraining a great many irregular thoughts and affections. Gill presses the inferiority harder: the disciple is not merely not above but below his master, in reputation as in knowledge, and cannot look for the same respect, so that if his master is not treated with the decency he deserves the disciple must not count it a hardship to be treated the same way.

Why the comparison is offered as comfort is Chrysostom’s subject. Loss of character, he observes, is to many the most grievous of all calamities, and it is one his disciples were to suffer among the rest; so Christ consoles them from his own case and from what had been said of him, a comfort he says no other can match. Hilary heightens that into something to be embraced: the Lord, the eternal Light and Captain of the faithful and Parent of immortality, sets this solace before them, that being made like him in suffering should be counted their glory. Remigius identifies the terms, Christ naming himself master and lord and his apostles disciples and servants, and explains how the sentence connects with what follows by its sharper form about the master of the house — as much as to say that they will not seek worldly honours while they see him pursuing the redemption of mankind through mockery. The Gloss puts the same in the second person, that they should not be indignant at suffering what he suffers too, since he is their lord, who does what he wills, and their master, who teaches what he knows to be profitable for them.

On the name itself the explanations agree. Jerome identifies it as the idol of Accaron, called the god of flies in the book of Kings, the first part of the name meaning idol and the second a fly; and he notes the fitness of calling the prince of the daemons after the foulest of idols, named from the uncleanness of the fly that spoils the sweetness of ointment. Barnes gives the same derivation and the same place, and supplies the application: they had called the Master and Teacher by that name, and the household must expect to be called it too.
25:
What the sufficiency amounts to is read as both comfort and rebuke. Gill takes it generously: a disciple should think himself well off and be thankful if he meets no worse treatment than his master, since the same honour would be more than he could expect and the same ill usage need not surprise him. Ellicott hears a tone of grave and tender sympathy, with a gentle play of feeling in the words, and makes the point simply — to be as their Master in anything, even in shame and suffering, might well be enough for any scholar. Clarke turns it into a series of questions pressed on the reader: can anyone pretending to be Christ’s scholar expect good treatment from the world, which loves its own and only its own, and why then so much impatience under suffering, such an excessive sense of injuries, such delicacy? Can you expect anything better from the world than you receive? Wesley enters a precise limitation on the comparison that follows, that the words cannot refer to the quantity of reproach and persecution, since in that the servant cannot exceed his lord, but only to its certainty.

Calvin reads the master-and-lord language for the claim it makes. To speak so is equivalent to calling himself Lord of the Church, as the apostle does when he compares him with Moses and the prophets and makes them servants where he is the Son and heir; and although he grants his people the honour of brotherhood, he remains the firstborn and head of the whole church, holding supreme government and power. From which Calvin concludes that nothing could be more unreasonable than the wish he is about to deny.

The name of reproach is where the philologists spread out. Ellicott notes that the Greek gives a form ending differently from the familiar one and says its history illustrates some interesting phases of Jewish thought, beginning from the form meaning lord of flies, probably as the power that sent or averted swarms of them. Robertson lists three spellings across the manuscripts and declines to settle the etymology, canvassing lord of a dwelling — which would make a pun on the master of the house in this very verse — and lord of flies, lord of dung, and lord of idolatrous sacrifices; whichever it is, he says it is plainly a term of reproach, and quotes the judgment that few words have given commentators more trouble.
26:
What the fearlessness rests on is answered in two quite different ways. Chrysostom denies that the saying is a general maxim at all and ties it strictly to what precedes: if being reviled grieves them, let them consider that in a little while they will be delivered from it, for men call them impostors and sorcerers and seducers now, but with a little patience all men will call them the saviours of the world. Gill reads it the same way, that time would bring everything to light and the wickedness of these men, now covered with specious pretences of sanctity and zeal for religion, would be seen through. Barnes makes the vindication the point, that their innocence and principles and integrity, though the world would not then acknowledge them, would be revealed in due time. Jerome pushes the horizon out instead: asked how it is that in the present world the sins of so many stay unknown, he answers that the saying speaks of the time to come, when God shall judge the hidden things of men, enlighten the hidden places of darkness and make manifest the secrets of hearts — so that the cruelty of the persecutor and the rage of the blasphemer are not to be feared, a day of judgment being appointed. Hilary agrees that neither threatening nor evil speaking nor the power of enemies should move men who know that the judgment day will disclose how empty all of it was. Origen supplies the scene from Daniel, the books opened and the judgment set, so that a record is kept of everything spoken and done and thought, and every hidden thing is manifested by divine power.

Calvin and Remigius both find a wider promise in the words. Calvin sets the apostles’ probable discouragement first — seeing the gospel so despised and the believers so few, they might throw away hope for the future — and has Christ meet the doubt by declaring that the gospel would spread widely, rise above every human hindrance and become generally known; he allows the sentence the appearance of a proverb but restricts it in a special way to that subject. Remigius reports the reading of those who take the words as a promise that through the apostles all the hidden mysteries lying under the veil of the letter of the Law should be revealed. Barnes likewise suspects the clause was a current Jewish proverb before it was used here.

The next clause is given both a local and a spiritual gloss. Rabanus explains the housetops from the custom of Palestine, where men sat on roofs that were flat rather than pointed, so that preaching on the housetops means speaking in the hearing of everyone. The Gloss reads the contrast as one of stages: what is said to them while they are still held under carnal fear they are to speak in the confidence of truth once the Spirit has enlightened them, and what they have merely heard they are to preach by doing it. Clarke draws the double edge of the whole passage, that God sees everything, which is consolation to the upright and dismay to the wicked, since he will bring every work and every secret thing into judgment, good or bad. Wesley puts the same in a line, that however men slander them now their innocence will at length appear.
27:
Two Jewish customs are heard behind the two halves of the verse. Lightfoot explains the ear from the practice of the schools, where the teacher whispered from his chair into the ear of an interpreter who then repeated aloud to the whole school what had been spoken privately, and he names an instance of such an interpreter standing as another man’s expositor. Wesley reports the same custom and adds the second, that the low flat roofs of their houses were sometimes used to preach to the people from. Barnes says simply that the flat roof was a public and conspicuous place. Rabanus had explained the same from the usage of the province, where men sat on roofs that were flat rather than pointed.

What the darkness and the whisper refer to is read as a feature of Christ’s own method. Ellicott takes the words to point both to the manner of his teaching and to the fact that it was reserved for a chosen few, and to them only as they were able to bear it: parables and dark sayings and whispered hints and many-sided proverbs were among the forms by which he led them on to truth, and in their own work as teachers they were not to shrink from publishing it through any fear. Barnes puts it plainly, that the private instructions given while he was with them were to be proclaimed publicly. Gill reads the verse as the ground of an open and faithful ministration without fear of the faces of men, since what had been hidden was not to remain so and they were the men appointed to reveal it — which, he notes, was the very purpose for which it had been communicated to them. Wesley compresses it into a sentence, that what is told secretly now is not to be kept secret long.

Clarke draws a boundary round the licence this might seem to give. A man ought to preach only what he has learned from God’s Spirit and his testimonies, and should not pretend to bring out anything new or mysterious; nothing concerning our salvation is newer than the new covenant, and in that, properly speaking, there are no mysteries at all, since what was formerly secret is now made manifest in the Gospel.
28:
The limit on the persecutor’s power is where every one of them begins. Barnes states it baldly: these are men, who have no power to injure the immortal part, and the body is a small matter beside the soul, temporal death a slight thing beside eternal, so that the direction is not to be alarmed at the prospect of the one but to fear him who can destroy both for ever. Clarke draws two conclusions from the same clause, that body and soul are distinct principles, since the body may be slain and the soul escape, and that the soul is immaterial, since the murderers of the body have it not in their power to injure it. Gill reads the verse as a description of bloody persecutors who, not content with reviling and scourging and imprisoning, put faithful ministers to death in the most torturing manner — and yet are not to be so dreaded as to divert them from their work, since, as Luke has it, after that they have no more that they can do. Calvin makes the argument turn on what a man was made for: this frail and perishing life ought to weigh little with men created for a heavenly immortality, so that if believers would consider for what purpose they were born they would have no reason to be so earnest in desiring an earthly life. He then puts the sharper half of it, that the fear of God is dead in men who fall from the confession of their faith through dread of tyrants, and that a brutish stupidity reigns in those who abandon it through dread of death.

The object of the fear commanded instead is disputed. Ellicott reports that few words have given rise to interpretations more strangely contrasted, since a number of devout and thoughtful commentators, unwilling to admit that our Lord ever presented the Father to men as a destroyer, have urged that the meaning is rather fear not men but the Spirit of Evil, the great Adversary, who has power to lead a man captive at his will if he yields to the temptation. Robertson rejects that reading outright: he reports the view that the devil as tempter is meant and not God as judge, and says surely its author is wrong, adding that there is no more needed lesson today than the fear of God. Clarke takes the same side in his own idiom, that it is not hell-fire we are to fear but God, without the stroke of whose justice hell itself would be no punishment and whose frown would make heaven insupportable. Wesley finds the command remarkable on its own account, that those who love God are told still to fear him, and under this very notion.

Two further notes concern the words. Ellicott observes that our Lord here uses what may be called the popular division of man’s nature, so that soul covers everything that truly lives and thinks and wills in him, answering to the fuller division of the apostle’s epistles. Robertson insists that destroy here is not annihilation but eternal punishment. Cyril uses the verse against the heretics, who make one God lord of the soul and another of the body and so leave neither of them perfect, each wanting what the other has; the clause confutes them, since unless the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has power over both, there is no explaining how he subjects both to punishment.
29:
The argument from the sparrows is set out the same way by all of them. Barnes names the two considerations, that God takes care of the smallest and least valuable of birds and that he numbers even the hairs of the head, and draws the inference that one who regards so small a thing will certainly provide for men. Jerome puts it as a contrast of natures: if these little creatures do not fall without God’s superintendence, and things made to perish do not perish without his will, then men who are immortal ought not to fear that they live outside his providence. Chrysostom gives the purpose of the image, that having set aside the fear of death he passes to the providence of God, lest the apostles should think that being put to death meant being deserted; and he enters a caution, that the hairs are mentioned not because God reckons them but to show his diligent knowledge and great carefulness over us. Robertson finds comfort in the phrase for everyone, Calvin the second of his consolations, that tyrants for all their madness have no power even over the body, so that it is improper to dread human cruelty as though one stood outside God’s protection.

The coin is worked out by the philologists. Clarke identifies the Roman coin as a tenth of the denarius and computes it at about three farthings of his own money, noting that the rabbis used the corresponding word for a thing of the lowest or almost no value. Ellicott distinguishes it from the farthing of another Gospel, which was a quarter of the same coin, and gives a fair approximation of its worth by observing that the denarius was the average day’s wages of a soldier or a labourer. Robertson calls the Greek a diminutive meaning any small bird, sparrows in particular, remarks that they are sold in the markets of Jerusalem and Jaffa to this day, and makes the coin slightly more than half an English penny. Gill supplies the Jewish reckoning, that a farthing was a very small coin, the ninety-sixth part of a shilling by their accounts, and sometimes equated with an Italian farthing worth eight of a still smaller unit.

The numbered hairs raise a question about the resurrection, and two of the fathers take it up. Augustine thinks it fair to ask whether all the hair ever shorn from us will return, since who would not dread such disfigurement; and he answers that once it is understood that nothing of the body is lost, so that the form and perfectness of all its parts is preserved, we understand at the same time that whatever would have disfigured it is to be taken up into the whole mass rather than fixed where it was. Jerome notes that those who deny the resurrection of the flesh ridicule this clause, and reads it instead as showing the boundless providence of God toward man and a care so unspeakable that nothing of ours is hidden from him. Remigius takes the hairs figuratively, Christ being the head and the apostles the hairs, well said to be numbered because the names of the saints are written in heaven. Hilary reads the selling figuratively too: what is sold is our soul and body and what it is sold to is sin, so that those who sell two sparrows for a farthing are the men who sell themselves for the smallest sin — born for flight, and for reaching heaven on spiritual wings, yet caught by the bait of present pleasures and bartering their whole selves away in such a market.
30:
The clause is taken as proverbial rather than literal.
