Gill calls it a proverbial expression showing the perfect knowledge God has and the exquisite care he takes in providence over all his creatures, and particularly over men, and most of all over his own children and faithful ministers — so that as no sparrow, so no single hair of a man’s head falls to the ground without his knowledge and will. Ellicott makes the same judgment in different terms, calling the figure an apparent hyperbole which is nevertheless the natural expression of a real thought, that even the incidents of life which seem most trivial are in very deed working together for good to those who love God; and he draws the practical inference, that they are not at any moment of their lives to think themselves uncared for by their Father.

Barnes presses the arithmetic of it rather than the figure. Each hair has engaged the care and attention of God, who has fixed the number; and though the matter is of small importance in itself he does not count it beneath him to determine how few or how many they shall be — from which the conclusion follows that he will take care of the men whose hairs they are. Clarke states the same with a distinction that carries the weight of his note: nothing is more astonishing than God’s care for his followers, since the least circumstances of their life are regulated not merely by that general providence which extends to all things, but by a particular providence which fits and directs everything to the design of their salvation and makes it all co-operate to that end.

Henry reads the clause as the second half of an argument whose first half was the sparrows, moving from the general extent of providence to the particular cognizance it takes of Christ’s disciples, and especially of their sufferings. He agrees that the expression is proverbial, denoting the account God keeps of everything that concerns his people, even what is most minute and least regarded; and he marks off the right use of it from the wrong, that it is not to be made a matter of curious enquiry but of encouragement to live in continual dependence on a providential care which reaches to every occurrence — and reaches so, he is careful to add, without any disparagement to the infinite glory, or disturbance to the infinite rest, of the Eternal Mind.
31:
The inference is drawn from the two previous images together. Gill joins them: they are neither to be afraid of men nor to distrust the providence of God, since if that providence reaches to the meanest of creatures and to the thing of least account about a man, it must far more regard the lives of men, and more still such useful lives as the disciples’ were. Robertson notes only the grammar, that the comparison stands in the ablative. Calvin distinguishes two grounds of the valuation and will not let them be confused: in a general way the saying is true of all men, since the lesser creatures were made for their advantage, but the discourse here belongs peculiarly to the sons of God, who hold a far higher right than any they derive from creation — and even the rank that belongs to men as men, he adds, arises solely from the undeserved kindness of God.

Clarke turns the comparison into an estimate nobody can make. None can reckon the value of a soul for which Christ has given his blood and his life, and the proper response is confidence in his goodness, since he who purchased so dearly will preserve and save. He then takes issue with a famous line of verse on the same subject, asking whether the poet meant to contradict Christ when he wrote of a God who sees with equal eye a hero perish or a sparrow fall — the point of the verse before him being precisely that the two are not of equal account.

Henry works the same comparison through the figure of the fowler. A bird does not fall into the net, or by the shot, and so come to be sold in the market, except as providence directs; and the disciples’ enemies are subtle fowlers who lay snares and shoot privily at them, yet can neither take them nor hit them unless God gives them leave — so that death is not to be feared, since such enemies have no power but what is given from above, and God can break their bows and snares and make the soul escape as a bird. He grants the valuation to all men, since the other creatures were made for man and put under his feet, and then presses it much further for the disciples of Christ, who are the excellent ones of the earth however much they are despised, as though not worth a single sparrow; and he sums the matter up by saying there is enough in the doctrine of providence to silence all the fears of God’s people.
32:
What confession means is defined with some care. Barnes notes that the same Greek word is rendered both confess and profess elsewhere, and takes it to mean acknowledging Christ, and our dependence on him for salvation, and our attachment to him, in every proper manner — a profession that may be made in uniting with a church, at the communion, in conversation and in conduct. Clarke makes it both inward and outward: whoever acknowledges him as the Messiah and has his heart and life regulated by his spirit and doctrine, since it is not enough to have the heart right before God but there must be a firm and manly and public profession before men — and he has short work with the man who says he is no hypocrite and will keep his religion to himself. Gill allows that the public confession here chiefly meant may include the less public one which every believer must make, since it is not enough to believe with the heart but confession must be made with the mouth. Wesley defines it as publicly acknowledging him for the promised Messiah, and insists the confession implies receiving his whole doctrine and obeying all his commandments. Remigius grounds the necessity in the apostle’s formula, that with the heart men believe unto justification and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation, and observes that Christ guards against anyone supposing he could be saved without the confession of the mouth by adding the words before men.

The promise answering it is read as a claim as much as a reward. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as making his confession in and for Christ, and the answering clause the same way, and points the promise forward to the day when the Son of Man shall be enthroned and shall acknowledge his faithful servants before his Father and the angels; he calls the words remarkable for the calmness with which they assert that final sovereignty. Robertson identifies the construction as an Aramaic rather than a Hebrew idiom, which reproduced literally in Greek means to confess in him, and finds in it a sense of unity between Christ and the man who takes an open stand for him. Chrysostom reads the whole verse as the next stage of consolation, since having banished their fear Christ now adds the hope of greater rewards to encourage a free proclamation of the truth, and he too notices that the Greek is not properly shall confess me. Hilary states the symmetry plainly, that in the measure we have borne witness to him on earth we shall have him bear witness to us in heaven before the face of the Father.

Two further notes concern who is being confessed, and to whom. Rabanus observes that not even pagans can deny that God exists, but unbelievers may deny that the Son is God as the Father is; and he explains why the Son confesses men before the Father, since it is by the Son that we have access to the Father, and it is the Son who says come, ye blessed of my Father. Calvin applies to this subject what had been said generally about the contempt of death: we must struggle against the dread of it so that it may not drive us back from the open confession of faith which God strictly demands and the world cannot endure, for which purpose the disciples of Christ must be bold enough to be always ready for martyrdom.
33:
What denial consists in is defined by its acts. Gill lists them: denying that one is a disciple of Christ and that Christ is one’s Lord and master, acting contrary to him, delivering things repugnant to his mind and will — which, he adds, was reckoned a heinous crime among the Jews for any disciple to do to his teacher. Clarke defines it by what is preferred instead: whoever puts his worldly interest above his duty to God, values earthly things more than heavenly, and chooses the friendship of men over the approbation of God. Robertson notes the change of construction from the previous verse and reads the accusative as a case of extension, a saying of no to Christ and a complete breach; he insists the sentence states a solemn law and not a mere social matter, the cleavage being public and final. Wesley adds only that it is a denial to which they would be strongly tempted.

The symmetry of the threat is what the others dwell on. Ellicott puts it as a general principle, that as with all eternal laws the blessing on those who meet the condition has its counterpart of woe on those who do not, so that to deny Christ on earth by word or deed, and to live as if his work were nothing to us, must lead to his denying us on the last day. Clarke states the consequence in its starkest form, that to be renounced by Christ is to have him neither for Mediator nor for Saviour, and so to appear before the tribunal of God without an Advocate. Remigius had already noted how the two halves are built alike, Christ adding the words before men to the denial as he had added them to the confession, so that no one should suppose the inward state enough by itself in either direction.

Henry sets the two verses together as one promise with its reverse, that Christ will shortly, in the day of triumph, own those who own him now in the day of trial, while those who deny him shall be for ever disowned and rejected. He makes the confession a duty rather than a feat of courage: it is not enough to believe in Christ, but that faith must be professed, in suffering for him when we are called to it as much as in serving him, so that we are never to be ashamed of our relation to him, our attendance on him, or our expectations from him. By that profession, Henry says, the sincerity of our faith is evidenced, his name glorified and others edified; and whatever reproach it brings now will be abundantly recompensed at the resurrection of the just.
34:
The saying is read as a paradox that needs the right definition of peace. Clarke says the difficulty clears once we consider what the word meant and what the Jews expected, since the Hebrew term the Greeks rendered here was used to express every possible blessing, temporal and spiritual. Gill supplies the expectation itself, that the Jews looked for great outward peace and prosperity in the days of the Messiah on the strength of prophecies they had misunderstood, and that the disciples had taken up the same notion, so that Christ thought fit to tell them the contrary. Barnes traces the words to a prophecy of Micah and makes the crucial distinction, that Christ did not mean the object of his coming was to produce discord, since he was the Prince of peace, but that discord would be one of its effects. Ellicott makes the same distinction more finely: Christ is our peace and came as the one great Peacemaker, yet the foreseen consequences of his work involved strife, and a consequence freely accepted for the sake of the greater good beyond it does in fact amount to a purpose. Wesley draws the same line, that division is not the design of his coming though it is the event of it.

Chrysostom faces the sharpest form of the objection, which is the Gospel against itself: how could he enjoin them to say peace be to this house, and how did the angels sing of peace on earth? His answer is a definition — that peace is most perfect when the diseased part is cut away and what introduces strife is removed, since only so can heaven and earth be joined. Jerome gives the historical form of the division, that in the matter of belief in Christ the whole world was set against itself and every household had its believers and its unbelievers. Lightfoot grants that reading as true and then presses a narrower one, that all interpreters observe the division between believers and unbelievers but the words point first and properly, as with a finger, at those horrid slaughters and civil wars among the Jews themselves which no other age saw and no history records. Rabanus states the principle in a line, that no mutual rights can be preserved between men at war in their creeds.

The sword itself is taken figuratively by the rest. Hilary notes that a sword is the sharpest of weapons and therefore the emblem of the right of authority, the impartiality of justice and the correction of offenders, and recalls that the word of God is elsewhere likened to one — so that the sword sent on the earth here is his preaching poured into the heart of man. The Gloss connects the verse backward to the warnings before it, that as the fear of death ought not to draw them away, neither ought carnal affection; on a second reading it makes the sword the Spirit’s, by which such affections are cut off rather than strengthened. Augustine allegorises the particular pairs, so that a man set against his father renounces the Devil whose son he was, and a daughter against her mother is the people of God against the city of the world, that wicked society which Scripture names Babylon and Egypt and Sodom. Gregory turns the household enmity into strategy on the enemy’s part: driven out of the hearts of the good, the subtle adversary seeks out those who love them most and speaks by the mouths of the dearest, so that while the heart is open with affection the sword of conviction may reach the inmost defences of virtue.
35:
The verse is taken as the explanation of the sword just mentioned. Gill says so directly, that here our Lord opens what he meant by it — intestine divisions, domestic broils and family differences, as well as the divisions that show themselves in towns and cities and kingdoms; and he prefers the rendering that a man is divided from his father. Robertson gives the verb its literal force, to divide in two, and notes that Christ is using Micah to describe the rottenness of the age as the prophet had done; the lesson he draws is that family and social ties cannot stand in the way of loyalty to Christ and righteous living. He also glosses the third relationship, where the Greek word is literally bride, the young wife who may be living in her mother-in-law’s house, and calls such a division a tragedy to witness.

Clarke locates the opposition in the spirits rather than the persons. The spirit of Christ can have no union with the spirit of the world, so that even a father, while unconverted, will oppose a godly child; the spirit in those who sin against God stands opposed to the spirit in his followers, and it is these that are at variance rather than the men themselves. Calvin uses the verse to confirm what he had argued earlier, that wars and tumults arise contrary to the nature of the Gospel and through the fault of wicked men; and he applies to all Christ’s ministers what Malachi had said of the Baptist, that they are sent for the opposite purpose, so that it is the malice of wicked men which turns those formerly united against each other the moment they hear.

Ellicott alone asks whether particular households were in view. He grants the words are partly an echo of the prophet, but thinks the choice of these three relationships as typical instances suggests a personal application, and puts the possibilities as questions: whether Zebedee had looked with displeasure on the calling of his two sons, whether there was variance between daughter-in-law and mother-in-law in Peter’s household, and how matters stood with the brethren of the Lord who as yet did not believe.
36:
Who the household foes are is specified by Gill. He names the children and the servants, those a man has either begotten and brought up or feeds daily at his table and maintains; and he notes that this instance, with those before it, is borrowed from the prophet, so that the times of the Gospel are set out in the same dismal and black characters as the age the prophet himself lived in. Wesley narrows the man in question to one who loves and follows Christ, which makes the enmity a consequence of discipleship rather than a general observation about families.

Clarke supplies what none of the others do, which is the Jewish expectation the saying answers to. He reports that our Lord is referring to their own traditions, and quotes one of the tracts for the prediction that a little before the coming of the Messiah the son shall insult the father, the daughter rebel against her mother and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and each man shall have his own household for his enemies; and he cites a second tract to the same effect about the age in which the Messiah comes. The effect of the citation is to show that the words would have struck the first hearers not as a paradox but as a recognised mark of the time they were waiting for — which is the point Gill reaches by another road when he traces the language back to the prophet. Clarke goes further and makes the correspondence an argument: he quotes a second tract for the age in which the young shall turn the elders into ridicule and the elders rise against the youth, the man of that age being excessively impudent and the son withholding reverence from his father; he calls these remarkable sayings, and holds that by them our Lord showed himself the Messiah, since all of it took place literally soon after his final rejection — for which he refers the reader to Josephus’s terrible account of those desolations.

Clarke then turns the verse inward, following Quesnel, so that the household enmity becomes a charge against the household itself. A father is his son’s enemy when by a bad education, an irregular love and a cruel indulgence he leaves him to take a wrong bias, instructs him not in his duty, and fills his mind with ambitious views; and the fault runs the other way in its turn. Read so, the saying describes not merely what persecution does to families but what families do to themselves.
37:
Why the comparison is introduced at all is Jerome’s question. Having spoken of a sword and not peace, Christ adds this lest anyone suppose that family affection was banished from his religion; and Jerome supplies the governing principle from the Song of Songs, that love is to be ordered, since such an order is needed in every affection. The Gloss notices the direction in which the comparison moves: since it commonly happens that parents love children more than children love parents, Christ, having taught that his love is to be preferred before the love of parents, goes on by an ascending scale to teach that it is to be preferred before the love of children too.

What the preference does not license is guarded carefully. Chrysostom takes up the apparent conflict with the apostle’s charge to obey parents in all things and says we need not marvel at it, since the obedience commanded is in such things as are not hurtful to our piety toward God: it is holy to render them every other honour, but when they demand more than is due we ought not to yield. He adds that this agrees with the older Scriptures, where the same Lord commands both the honour and its limit. Rabanus states the rule in its negative form, that a man is unworthy of the divine communion who prefers the carnal affection of kindred to the spiritual love of God.

What unworthiness means here is read eschatologically. Hilary says those who have valued the affection of relations above God are unworthy to inherit the good things to come, and then turns to the second clause of the saying by way of the apostle’s words, that those who are Christ’s have crucified the body with its vices and lusts — so that a man is unworthy of Christ who does not take up his cross, in which we suffer with him and die with him and are buried and rise again with him. Gill takes the plainer sense throughout, that the one who will not prefer Christ to the nearest relation is pronounced no fit disciple, which is the same verdict the chapter has been working toward from the warning about household enemies onward.
38:
The image is explained from Roman practice before it is applied. Barnes describes the sentence passed on those condemned to crucifixion, part of which was that they should carry to the place of execution the cross they were to die on, as Christ carried his until exhaustion overtook him, and he describes the instrument itself as two rough beams of wood joined together. Clarke gives the same custom and supports it from Plutarch, and reads the clause accordingly: a man not ready, after Christ’s example, to suffer death in the cause of his religion does not deserve to be called his disciple. Robertson notes that this is the first mention of a cross in this Gospel, that criminals were crucified at Jerusalem, and that the condemned man ordinarily bore his own until Simon of Cyrene was pressed into the service; he adds that the Jews had been familiar with crucifixion since the days of Antiochus Epiphanes. Ellicott doubts the words were a specific announcement of the manner of our Lord’s own death, though he grants that read by the event they imply a distinct prevision of it, and thinks what they would recall to the disciples was the sad sight Roman rule had made familiar, the procession of robbers or rebels each carrying his own.

What the cross stands for is widened by the rest. Gill takes it for all sorts of afflictions, reproaches and persecutions, and death itself, and particularly for the ill will and hatred of near relations which must be expected by anyone who bears a faithful testimony. Wesley defines it narrowly and usefully as whatever pain or inconvenience cannot be avoided except by doing some evil or omitting some good. Gregory distinguishes two ways of bearing it, either by afflicting the flesh with abstinence or by making a neighbour’s afflictions our own in compassion; and he enters a caution, that some make a show of abstinence not for God but for ostentation. Calvin reads the verse as the move from particular cases to the general rule, that we cannot be reckoned Christ’s disciples unless we are prepared to endure many afflictions — so that when we are vexed by the thought of the gospel setting us at variance with father or wife or children, this is the condition to remember.

Cyril, on the other hand, uses the occasion to protect what the saying might seem to overthrow. While we honour our heavenly Father we are to honour the fathers of our flesh as well, since the Lord himself appointed it plainly in the Law and the Prophets, promising that it should be well with the man who honours his father and mother and that his days should be long in the land; and Cyril presses that commandment especially on the hearers before him.
39:
The paradox turns on two senses of a single word, and they all say so. Barnes states the two plainly, that whoever is anxious to save his temporal life, or his comfort and security here, shall lose eternal life, while whoever is willing to risk or lose his comfort and life here for Christ’s sake shall gain it. Ellicott notes that the word is the same one rendered soul earlier in the chapter, meaning that by which a man lives in either the lower or the higher sense, and that the whole point lies in the contrast: to gain the lower now is to lose the higher hereafter, and the reverse. Remigius had made the same distinction, that life here is not the substance of the soul but this present state of being, so that the man who so loves this light and its joys as to wish always to find them shall lose the very thing he wished to keep. Wesley compresses the whole into a sentence, that he who saves his life by denying Christ loses it eternally and he who loses it by confessing him saves it eternally.

Gill and Clarke both take the saying as a description of actual conduct. Gill has in view the man who seeks to preserve his life and its temporal enjoyments by a sinful compliance with his friends and the world, and by denying Christ or failing to confess him. Clarke puts the same and adds a historical instance which he says fulfilled the words literally, the case of Archbishop Cranmer, who confessed Christ and then recanted to save his life and lost it notwithstanding. Robertson observes that the paradox appears in four forms across the Gospels and calls it one of the profound sayings Christ repeated many times, noting a near parallel in the Hebrew of one of the wisdom books about the man who gives his life and finds her.

Calvin explains why the saying is added where it is. The preceding doctrine is difficult and troublesome to the flesh and might carry little weight with us, so Christ confirms it in two ways at once: men of excessive caution and foresight, just when they think they have defended themselves best, will be disappointed and lose what they guarded, while those who disregard their own safety will keep it. The two halves of the sentence are therefore not a riddle but a warning and a promise set side by side.
40:
Why the promise comes at this point is Jerome’s question, and he puts it as a practical one. Christ had taken gold from his preachers and shaken brass out of their purses, which makes the preacher’s condition hard — whence then their living, their food, their necessaries? So he tempers the charge with this, and makes those who receive them responsible for their keep. Chrysostom reaches the same point from the other side: enough had already been said to persuade anyone who should have to entertain them, since who would not gladly take into his house men so courageous that they despised every danger so that others might be saved; and where he had earlier threatened punishment on those who would not receive them, he now promises reward to those who do.

How much the reception amounts to is pressed as far as it will go. Hilary reads the verse as showing Christ’s mediatorial office, since he came from God, so that when he is received God is thereby transfused into us; and by this disposition of grace to have received the apostles is nothing other than to have received God, because Christ dwells in them and God in Christ. Gregory works on the exact wording of the clause about the prophet, noting that it says not a reward from a prophet but the reward of a prophet; and he explains the difference, that a prophet is perhaps a righteous man, and the less he owns in this world the more confidence he has in speaking for righteousness, so that the man who has this world’s goods and supports him makes himself a free partaker in the other’s work.

The moderns keep to the chain of identification. Clarke puts it in the first person, that to treat them kindly is to welcome Christ, who will count the courtesy as shown to himself. Ellicott notes that a discourse which had spoken so plainly of suffering ends with promise and the assurance of victory, and grounds the chain in the sending: as Christ was sent by the Father, so were these men his apostles and representatives, and any honour or affection paid them he would reckon as paid to himself, and through him to his Father. Calvin calls it another consolation, fit to move a great many people to treat them kindly, since whatever is done to them Christ does not scruple to count as done to himself — which shows, Calvin says, how dearly he loves them. Barnes reads all three illustrations as teaching substantially one thing, that anyone hospitable to Christ, to his disciples, to a prophet or to an upright man declares by it that he approves their character, and will not go unrequited. Gill explains why the comfort was needed just here, lest from the catalogue of sorrows and persecutions the disciples should conclude that nobody would take them in or listen to their message. Remigius adds a reading that raises the stakes, that some understand the prophet here to be the Lord Jesus Christ himself, of whom Moses said that a Prophet should be raised up, and the righteous man likewise, as being beyond comparison righteous.
41:
What kind of prophet is meant has to be settled first, and all of them settle it the same way. Gill says the word means not a foreteller of things to come but a preacher of the Gospel, and that welcoming such a man involves not merely embracing his doctrine but lodging and keeping him generously. Clarke agrees the term denotes a teacher rather than a seer, since that is not always its sense, and describes him as commissioned by God to publish the doctrines of eternal life; he calls it no small distinction to lodge a minister of Christ under one’s roof, and sharpens the point by a contrast — few are admitted to exercise that sacred office, but none are shut out from sharing its benefits. Wesley compresses both definition and consequence into a line: whoever lodges such a preacher precisely because he is one will share his recompense.

The phrase about the name is where the exactness lies. Ellicott explains it as meaning for the sake of what the title implies, namely the office of a messenger of God, of which righteousness the upright man alive before us is the concrete instance; and he finds in the difference between the two titles a higher inspiration attaching to the messenger, which he suspects may have belonged to some of the Twelve and not to all. Robertson renders the idiom as because he is a prophet and supports it from a papyrus of the first century which uses the same construction for being free-born; and he quotes the judgment that a host moved by no ulterior motive, but simply by what his visitor is, would obtain in the coming age a recompense equal to his guest’s.

Calvin reads the verse as the beginning of a descent. Christ begins at the top with God’s messengers and descends at length to the lowest rank, taking in all his disciples, and so commends without exception everyone who truly worships God and loves the gospel; and Calvin marks the limit of the principle, that although God enjoins offices of kindness toward all mankind, what is singled out here is kindness done for the sake of the doctrine and out of respect to piety.

Who the little ones are is agreed, and the title is read as deliberate. Gill traces the descent of the whole passage, from prophets to righteous men and from righteous men to those of the lowest class among them, who have the least measure of grace and spiritual light and are outwardly the poorest and most contemptible in the eyes of the world. Barnes says they are clearly the disciples, called little to denote their want of wealth and rank and learning and whatever else the world calls great, little in the world’s estimation and in their own, learners and not yet teachers, making no pretension to what attracts admiration. Clarke calls them his apparently mean and generally despised disciples, and Wesley reduces the phrase to the very least Christian. Ellicott adds the usage behind it, that the term was familiarly used of the scholars of a Rabbi, and that our Lord, as the great Master sending out his disciples, employs it in that sense.

The cup is handled both textually and morally. Clarke reports that the word for water is absent from the common text but present in a long list of manuscripts and versions and in Origen, and holds it necessarily understood, the same ellipsis being frequent in Greek and Latin writers. Ellicott puts the force of the clause as a limit on what may be disregarded: Christ would not overlook even a cup of cold water given to the humblest disciple as such and for his own sake. The Gloss states the principle the example rests on, that God looks more to the pious mind of the giver than to the abundance of what is given; and it offers a second reading of the title, that the least are those who have nothing at all in this world and shall yet be judges with Christ.

Taken with the two verses before it, the saying completes a scale on which no kindness is too small to be counted. The prophet and the righteous man have their proper rewards, and then the scale runs down to a drink of water given to the least of the disciples — which is why Gill can describe the movement as a gradual descent, and why Ellicott can insist that the words, taken by themselves, go no further than this.
